newsitem.title: INDIA: Likely tax breaks, reform hopes spur Indian bourses.
newsitem.headline: Likely tax breaks, reform hopes spur Indian bourses.

text.p: India's stock market is riding high on expectations of tax breaks and government promises to pursue economic reforms and woo foreign investment, analysts said on Friday.
"The rally is built on expectations," said a senior vice president of the Indian affiliate of a foreign broking firm. "To that extent the market is vulnerable."
The fund manager, who asked not be identified, said he expected the government to reform taxes by reviving concessions that encouraged companies to save cash for expansion or diversification.
Other expectations include the exemption of dividends from taxes and the scrapping of a controversial minimum alternate tax (MAT) imposed in last July's budget.
Some traders hope the government will give excise relief to industries like cement, steel and consumer goods that are hit by a slowdown in demand and a squeeze on margins.

M.R. Madhavan, market strategist at ICICI Securities and Finance Company Ltd (I-Sec), said companies were likely to be allowed to buy back their own shares from stockholders, reducing the capital base and boosting values.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said recently the government would announce measures on January 15 to revive industrial growth and depressed stock markets.
But The Business Standard newspaper on Friday quoted Deve Gowda as saying the policy initiatives would be delayed until the first week of February.
The top-30 share benchmark index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE), the country's premier bourse, finished on Friday at a provisional 3,416.17 points -- up 10.73 percent since the close of 1996.
Compared to a three-year low of 2,713.12 reached on December 4, the index was up 703.05 points, or 25.91 percent.
Analysts said the upsurge was due to switching of funds from cash assets to equities because of a decline in interest rates and attractive share valuations.
"This is a valuation-driven broader market rally," said Ajit Verma, senior analyst with Asian Capital Partners, a foreign securities firm. "It looks good to sustain."
But I-Sec's Madhavan said the signals were confusing and the rally was likely to peter out.
"I'm not particularly bullish," he said. "The fundamentals look bleak... second half (company) results will be worse than the first half. We might even see negative growth."
He said increases in government-controlled prices of petroleum products were inevitable. These would hit most industries through higher fuel, power and transportation costs.
Madhavan attributed the stocks rally to front-running by big local players in anticipation of higher foreign allocations into emerging markets like India.

"Higher funds inflow can drive the market up," he said. "But in the longer run this market has to come down. It has to reflect domestic economic factors. Most commodities are still to see a turnaround."
